extra.message: Server-side template injection via Jinja2 Template-from-string — Remote code execution via Jinja2 SSTI payload [verified: Attacker-controlled `fragment` is concatenated into a Jinja2 template string and rendered, giving classic SSTI/RCE via `{{ }}` payloads.]

OS command injection via ping host parameter — Arbitrary OS command execution as the application user [verified: `host` GET param is concatenated unsanitized into a shell string passed to os.system, allowing full command injection via shell metacharacters.]
OS command injection in ping probe endpoint — Arbitrary OS command execution as the application user [verified: Duplicate of idx 2 — same unsanitized os.system concatenation of `host`.]

Mass assignment lets patient self-reassign primary_clinician and is_active — Patient can silently reassign their own treating clinician (granting an arbitrary clinician access to their chart) or toggle their own active status via a form field never intended to be patient-editable. [verified: can_edit_demographics returns true for the patient themselves, and PatientDemographicsForm exposes primary_clinician and is_active with no field restriction, letting a patient reassign their own clinician or toggle active status.]

Mass assignment of patient/clinician/appointment fields in visit summary form bypasses authorization — A clinician who passes the initial check on their own appointment can submit a crafted POST with patient/clinician/appointment set to arbitrary IDs, creating a fraudulent clinical visit summary (diagnosis, care instructions, notes) attached to a patient they have no care relationship with. [verified: VisitSummaryForm binds 'patient','clinician','appointment' directly from POST overriding the initial dict, and views.py:286 saves with no re-check that submitted values match the authorized appointment/patient.]

Cross-patient prescription creation via unrestricted patient field + check-after-save — Any authenticated clinician can create prescriptions for patients outside their care team, corrupting medication records for arbitrary patients; the write persists even though the request is ultimately denied. [verified: PrescriptionForm exposes 'patient' as an unrestricted ModelChoiceField and form.save() persists the row before can_edit_clinical check runs at views.py:338, so the row exists regardless of the later PermissionDenied.]

Prescription created and persisted before ownership check; clinician field impersonation — Any clinician/clinic_admin can create a persisted prescription for a patient outside their care relationship and attribute it to an arbitrary clinician, corrupting clinical records and prescribing accountability. [verified: Same as idx0: form.save() at line 337 persists before the ownership check on line 338, and PrescriptionForm also exposes 'clinician' as an unrestricted ModelChoiceField allowing attribution to arbitrary providers.]

Weak shared-secret authentication gates high-privilege ops endpoints — A single leaked static token (e.g. via logging, git history, or timing side-channel on ==) grants unauthenticated RCE, command injection, and PII exfiltration across all ops endpoints [verified: _wrk_gate is a single static shared-secret compared with plain `==`, no rate limiting/rotation, gating ~18 dangerous endpoints — a genuine broken-authentication design flaw.]

Sensitive PII/secret exposure in ops response — Disclosure of SSN-like PII and a live partner integration secret to anyone holding the shared ops token [verified: Duplicate of idx 11's exposure half — hardcoded sync token and SSN-shaped tax_ref returned in plaintext JSON at line 48.]

Sensitive data (sync token, SSN-like PII, bearer token) exposed via ops endpoints and logs — Exposure of live partner sync token, SSN-like tax reference, and bearer tokens through ops responses and application logs, usable for account takeover or partner-system impersonation [verified: Hardcoded live-looking sync token and SSN-shaped tax_ref are returned in plaintext JSON (line 48), and the raw body plus Authorization header are logged at WARNING (lines 72-73) — both genuine sensitive-data exposure paths.]

Sensitive data (auth header, request body) written to logs — Credentials/tokens and PHI leak into log storage, accessible to anyone with log access [verified: Duplicate of idx 11's logging half — raw body and Authorization header logged verbatim at WARNING.]

Code injection via eval() of user-controlled expression — Remote code execution / sandbox escape via crafted eval() expression [verified: eval() runs an attacker-controlled `expr` string; stripping __builtins__ is a well-known incomplete sandbox (attribute-chain escapes via str/format/etc. exist), and the endpoint is gated only by the shared static token which itself is weak.]

Missing authentication on ops identity-ping endpoint — Unauthenticated attacker can hit an internal ops endpoint that is supposed to require the shared ops token, potentially probing internal identity/notification workflow [verified: patient_identity_ping_339 (line 91) is the only handler in the file with no `_wrk_gate` call before use, and urls.py wires it to /ops/identity/patient-ping-339/ with no other decorator, so it's reachable unauthenticated.]

Path traversal in ops file-write endpoint — Arbitrary file write anywhere the app process can write (e.g. overwrite application code, cron scripts, or escape private_exports) via `../` in `name` [verified: `name` is joined onto BASE_EXPORT_DIR with no traversal sanitization (no resolve()/relative_to check), then request body is written to that path, permitting arbitrary file write via `../`.]

XXE via lxml parser with entity resolution enabled — Local file disclosure and SSRF via crafted DOCTYPE/external entity XML payloads [verified: Duplicate of idx 4 — same XXE-enabled parser configuration.]

NoSQL injection via unrestricted MongoDB filter — NoSQL injection allowing data exfiltration or, with `$where`, arbitrary JS execution in MongoDB [verified: The JSON body's `filter` (or whole body) is passed verbatim as a MongoDB query filter with no schema/type restriction, permitting operator injection like $where/$regex.]

Insecure hardcoded fallback Django SECRET_KEY — Forging of session cookies and CSRF tokens, potential full account takeover if deployed with default key [verified: SECRET_KEY hardcoded fallback 'dev-only-change-me' at settings.py:6, used directly with no strength check.]

DEBUG defaults to True in settings — Verbose Django debug pages leak source code, local variables, settings (including SECRET_KEY-adjacent config) and stack traces to any anonymous user who triggers an error [verified: DEBUG defaults to '1' (True) when DJANGO_DEBUG unset, confirmed at settings.py:7 with no other override.]

DEBUG defaults to True in production settings — Verbose error pages leak source code, settings values, environment variables, SQL queries, and in-memory PHI/session data to any user who triggers a server error [verified: Same DEBUG=True default as [0]; duplicate finding, same code evidence, valid for a PHI-handling app.]

Unvalidated assigned_provider on secure message thread creation — Patient can route a secure-messaging thread containing PHI to an arbitrary/unrelated clinician of their choosing, bypassing triage and potentially exposing sensitive message content to an unintended staff member. [verified: thread_create only restricts the 'patient' field queryset for patient role; assigned_provider is left fully form-editable and unchecked by can_view_patient, so a patient can route a thread to an arbitrary provider.]

Reflected XSS in ops notelet-card preview — Reflected XSS against any client that can reach this endpoint (e.g. via a leaked/guessed ops token, or if gate is bypassed) — arbitrary script execution in victim's browser session [verified: `copyline` GET param is concatenated unescaped into an HTML response with content_type text/html, allowing reflected XSS.]

Unvalidated financial ledger manipulation — Attacker can set arbitrary/negative amounts and force approval state, corrupting financial ledger integrity [verified: amount and state come straight from attacker JSON/GET with no bounds/validation and are applied to a balance/approval object, permitting arbitrary balance manipulation and forced approval.]

Open redirect via ops lane parameter — Phishing: attacker crafts a link through this trusted domain that redirects victims to an attacker-controlled site [verified: `lane` from GET/POST is passed directly to redirect() with no allow-list or scheme/host validation, enabling open redirect.]

Brute-forceable PIN verification with user enumeration — Attacker can enumerate valid handles and brute-force the 4-digit verifier to impersonate/queue actions as that handle [verified: handle/verifier check distinguishes 404 (unknown handle) from 403 (bad verifier) with no rate limiting on a 4-digit PIN space, enabling enumeration and brute force.]

CORS misconfiguration reflecting Origin with credentials allowed — Any malicious website can read authenticated ops responses cross-origin (data theft) if the caller's session/credentials are sent [verified: Origin header is reflected directly into Access-Control-Allow-Origin while Allow-Credentials is true — classic reflected-CORS-with-credentials misconfig, no allow-list.]

Privilege escalation via forgeable client-controlled badge cookie/header — Any caller who already has (or can guess) the shared ops token can further self-elevate to 'lead' access and read payroll/casework data by simply setting a cookie/header [verified: Elevated 'lead' access is granted purely by matching a client-supplied cookie/header string with no signature or server-side verification, allowing trivial self-elevation once the outer static token is known.]

TLS certificate verification disabled for outbound partner request — Man-in-the-middle attacker can intercept/tamper with partner status responses; combined with any user-influenced URL this becomes SSRF with no integrity guarantee [verified: ssl._create_unverified_context() is used for an outbound HTTPS call, disabling certificate/hostname verification entirely.]

TLS certificate verification disabled on outbound partner request — MITM attacker can intercept/tamper with partner communication [verified: Duplicate of idx 7 — same ssl._create_unverified_context() usage.]

TLS certificate verification disabled on outbound partner call — Susceptible to man-in-the-middle attacks on partner communications, undermining confidentiality/integrity of data exchanged [verified: Duplicate of idx 7 — same unverified SSL context on outbound partner call.]

Hardcoded default DB credentials and non-enforced TLS for Postgres — Weak/guessable default DB password if env vars aren't set, and DB traffic (including PHI) can be silently downgraded to unencrypted if a MITM strips TLS since sslmode=prefer doesn't enforce encryption [verified: DB credentials default to weak 'clinic_portal'/'clinic_portal' and sslmode defaults to 'prefer' (not 'require') at settings.py:50-56, allowing silent unencrypted fallback.]

Missing Secure cookie flags and SSL redirect enforcement — Session and CSRF cookies for patients/staff can be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP and captured by a network attacker, leading to session hijacking and access to PHI [verified: No SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE, CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE, or SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT anywhere in settings.py; only HTTPONLY/SAMESITE set at lines 82-85, confirming cookies can be sent over HTTP.]

API key accepted via GET query parameter leaks into logs — Long-lived ClinicAPIKey secrets logged in access/proxy logs or browser history can be captured and replayed by an attacker with log/history access, granting them the availability API's authenticated access. [verified: availability_api falls back to request.GET.get('api_key') when the header is absent, so the long-lived API key can end up in URLs/logs; genuinely present with no compensating control, though impact is limited to a non-PHI availability endpoint.]

Mass assignment of privileged fields via unrestricted dict update — Attacker-supplied JSON can flip privilege/role/limit fields in the response payload, indicating the same unrestricted-update pattern would escalate privileges if backed by a real persistence layer [verified: workset.update(change_set) merges the entire attacker JSON body into a privilege-shaped dict with no allow-list, though it's not backed by real persistence so impact is limited to the response payload — still a genuine mass-assignment pattern.]

Security headers explicitly disabled by ops endpoint — Weakens defense-in-depth against XSS for responses served from this endpoint [verified: patient_frame_slip_479 explicitly sets X-XSS-Protection to "0" and CSP to empty string, actively disabling browser-side XSS mitigations on that response.]
